stem: A delivery truck traveling forward at 24 m/s brakes steadily, slowing to 6.0 m/s in 9.0 s while still moving forward. Taking the forward direction as positive, what is the truck's average acceleration?

rationales.A: Computes the velocity change correctly (6.0 − 24 = −18 m/s) but does not divide by the 9.0 s, so a change in velocity is reported as an acceleration.
rationales.B: Adds the two speeds instead of finding their difference: (24 + 6.0)/9.0 = 30/9.0 ≈ 3.3 m/s², then attaches a negative sign because the truck slows. The velocity change is 6.0 − 24 = −18 m/s.
rationales.C: Subtracts in the wrong order, (24 − 6.0)/9.0 = +2.0 m/s². Average acceleration is the final velocity minus the initial velocity, divided by the time, so slowing down along the positive direction gives a negative value.
rationales.D: Average acceleration = (v − v₀)/Δt = (6.0 − 24)/9.0 = −18/9.0 = −2.0 m/s². The negative sign shows the acceleration points opposite the (forward) velocity.

stem: The Moon orbits Earth. Which force is the Newton's-third-law partner of Earth's gravitational force on the Moon?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Earth's gravitational force on the Sun

choices.label: B
choices.text: the Sun's gravitational force on the Moon

choices.label: C
choices.text: an outward force on the Moon, away from Earth, that balances Earth's pull

choices.label: D
choices.text: the Moon's gravitational force on Earth

rationales.A: This is a force on the Sun, from Earth, and it pairs with the Sun's pull on Earth. It does not involve the Moon, so it is not the partner of Earth's pull on the Moon.
rationales.B: This force acts on the Moon and comes from a different object (the Sun), so it is not an interaction between Earth and the Moon. The partner must be exerted by the Moon on Earth.
rationales.C: No such balancing outward force acts on the Moon; if one did, the net force would be zero and the Moon would move in a straight line. Also, the third-law partner of Earth's pull on the Moon must be a force exerted by the Moon on Earth, not another force on the Moon.
rationales.D: Third-law partners are equal in magnitude and opposite in direction and act on different objects. Earth pulls on the Moon, so the partner is the Moon pulling on Earth with a force of the same size.

stem: A child pulls a wagon 4.0 m along level ground with a constant 20 N force directed 60° above the horizontal. How much work does the child's pull do on the wagon?

rationales.A: Multiplies the full force by the full distance, 20 × 4.0 = 80 J, ignoring the angle. Only the component F cos 60° = 10 N is along the motion.
rationales.B: Only the component of force along the displacement does work: W = Fd cos 60° = 20 × 4.0 × 0.50 = 40 J.
rationales.C: Adds the quantities, 20 + 4.0 = 24. Work is the product of force component and displacement, not a sum.
rationales.D: Uses sin 60° instead of cos 60°: 20 × 4.0 × 0.866 = 69 J. That uses the vertical component of the force (F sin 60°), which is perpendicular to the displacement and does no work.

stem: A 60 kg climber ascends a cliff face, gaining 15 m in height. Use g = 10 m/s². The increase in the climber's gravitational potential energy is

rationales.A: Leaves out the mass and multiplies only g by the height: 10 × 15 = 150. That is not the climber's energy change, which is proportional to the 60 kg mass.
rationales.C: Multiplies only mass and height, 60 × 15 = 900, and leaves out g. The energy change needs the weight mg times the height gained.
rationales.D: Computes only the weight, mg = 60 × 10 = 600 N, and does not multiply by the 15 m of height gained.

stem: A tablecloth is yanked quickly out from under a vase, and the vase stays nearly in place. This happens mainly because

choices.label: A
choices.text: inertia resists changes in the vase's motion, and the cloth's force is brief

choices.label: B
choices.text: gravity holds the vase to the table, so friction cannot move it

choices.label: C
choices.text: the cloth exerts no force at all on the vase

choices.label: D
choices.text: the vase gains extra mass while the cloth slides

rationales.A: The vase tends to remain at rest (Newton's first law). The cloth acts on the vase for only a very short time, so the friction impulse is small and the vase's velocity barely changes.
rationales.B: Gravity does not prevent friction from acting; the vase would move if the friction force acted long enough. The vase stays nearly in place because of its inertia and the brief interaction.
rationales.C: The cloth does exert a friction force on the vase while it slides underneath; what limits the vase's motion is that the force acts for only a very short time. A force of zero is not required to explain why the vase barely moves.
rationales.D: The vase's mass does not change while the cloth slides. Its inertia is the same; the brief interaction just cannot change its motion much.

stem: A 10 kg cabinet rests on a floor with mu_s = 0.50 and mu_k = 0.30. A mover pushes horizontally with 20 N and the cabinet stays at rest. The mover then pushes with 35 N and the cabinet still stays at rest. Use g = 10 m/s^2. What is the magnitude of the friction force during the 35 N push?

rationales.A: This is the maximum static friction, 0.50 × 100 = 50 N. Friction reaches that value only when the push reaches 50 N; at 35 N the friction equals the push, 35 N.
rationales.B: This keeps the friction value from the first push; static friction increases to match the larger 35 N push.
rationales.C: The cabinet is at rest, so the net force is zero and static friction equals the push: 35 N (still below the maximum mu_s N = 50 N).
rationales.D: This is kinetic friction, 0.30 x 100 = 30 N, which applies only once the cabinet slides.

stem: A 1200 kg car crosses the lowest point of a dip in a road. The dip is a circular arc of radius 30 m, and the car moves at 15 m/s. Using g = 10 m/s², the normal force of the road on the car at that point is

rationales.A: Keeps only the centripetal term, N = mv²/r = (1200)(225)/30 = 9000 N, and leaves out the 12000 N needed just to balance the car's weight.
rationales.B: Sets N = mg, as if the car were in vertical equilibrium: (1200)(10) = 12000 N. The car accelerates toward the center of the arc, so N must exceed mg.
rationales.C: Take inward (toward the arc's center, which is above the car) as positive: N − mg = mv²/r, so N = mg + mv²/r = 12000 N + (1200)(15)²/30 N = 12000 N + 9000 N = 21000 N.
rationales.D: Uses mg − N = mv²/r, which takes the center of the circle to be below the car; N = 12000 − 9000 = 3000 N. At the lowest point of the dip the center is above the car, so the road's upward push must exceed the weight.

stem: A block on a frictionless table is attached to a horizontal ideal spring that is at its natural length when the block is at x = 0. The block is pulled from x = +0.10 m to x = +0.30 m. During this motion, the elastic potential energy stored in the spring

choices.label: A
choices.text: decreases because the spring is pulling the block

choices.label: B
choices.text: stays zero because the spring is at x = 0 in equilibrium

choices.label: C
choices.text: increases to 9 times its initial value

choices.label: D
choices.text: increases to 3 times its initial value

rationales.A: Confuses the direction of the force with the direction of the motion. The spring pulls toward x = 0 while the block moves away from it, so the spring does negative work and U increases.
rationales.B: Applies the equilibrium position to the whole motion. U = ½kx² is zero only at x = 0; at x = 0.10 m it is already 0.005k joules and at 0.30 m it is 0.045k joules.
rationales.C: U = ½kx², so U is proportional to x². Going from 0.10 m to 0.30 m multiplies x by 3, so U is multiplied by 3² = 9. The spring force points back toward x = 0, against the motion, so the spring does negative work.
rationales.D: Treats U as proportional to the stretch, giving 0.30/0.10 = 3. Since U = ½kx², the factor is 3² = 9.

stem: A small ball rolls along the inside of a vertical circular track. At one instant it is at the point on the right side of the track that is level with the center of the circle, and it is moving. What is the direction of the normal force exerted by the track on the ball at that instant?

choices.label: A
choices.text: Horizontal, pointing to the left toward the center of the circle

choices.label: B
choices.text: Vertically upward, to balance the ball's weight

choices.label: C
choices.text: Tangent to the track, pointing vertically downward

choices.label: D
choices.text: Horizontal, pointing to the right away from the center

rationales.A: The track is on the ball's right and the normal force is perpendicular to the surface, pushing the ball toward the center. At this point that is horizontal and to the left; it supplies the centripetal force while gravity acts downward.
rationales.B: The normal force is perpendicular to the surface of contact; at this point the track surface is vertical, so the normal force is horizontal, not vertical. The normal force here does not balance the weight.
rationales.C: A normal force is perpendicular to the surface, not tangent to it. At this point the tangent is vertical, and the downward pull there is gravity, not the normal force.
rationales.D: The track is on the ball's right side and can only push the ball away from the track surface, which is to the left. A rightward force would pull the ball into the track, which a normal force cannot do.

stem: An 800 kg car speeds up from 10 m/s to 20 m/s. What is the change in the car's kinetic energy?

rationales.A: This is the kinetic energy at the average speed, (1/2)(800)(15^2) = 90,000 J. The change in K is the difference of the kinetic energies at 20 and 10 m/s, not the K at the mean speed.
rationales.B: This is (1/2)m(Delta v)^2 = (1/2)(800)(20 - 10)^2 = 40,000 J. It squares the speed change instead of taking the difference of the squared speeds.
rationales.D: This is only the final kinetic energy, (1/2)(800)(20^2) = 160,000 J; the initial kinetic energy was not subtracted.

stem: A 0.50 kg ball slows from 12 m/s to 8 m/s while sliding across a rough floor. What is the change in the ball's kinetic energy?

rationales.A: This is only the final kinetic energy, (1/2)(0.50)(8^2) = 16 J; the initial kinetic energy was not subtracted.
rationales.B: This has the right size but the wrong sign. The ball slows, so its final kinetic energy is less than its initial one and Delta K is negative.
rationales.C: Delta K = (1/2)(0.50)(8^2) - (1/2)(0.50)(12^2) = 16 J - 36 J = -20 J. The negative sign shows the kinetic energy decreases.
rationales.D: This is (1/2)m(Delta v)^2 = (1/2)(0.50)(4)^2 = 4 J with a negative sign attached. The change in K is (1/2)m times the difference of the squared speeds, which is 20 J in size.
